facts.text: Tung trees were brought to Taiwan from China during the period of Japanese rule and were planted widely in Hakka hill areas as a cash crop.
Oil pressed from Tung seeds resists water; it was valued by makers of boats, furniture, and paper umbrellas, including the oil-paper umbrellas of Meinong.
Tung wood was made into furniture, wooden sandals, toothpicks, and matchsticks.
The fruit of the Tung tree cannot be eaten because it is poisonous.
Tung oil and wood were important sources of income for many Hakka families, but Tung oil production has since declined.
Tung trees bloom from April to May in Hakka areas in the hills of northern and central Taiwan.
The white Tung flowers that cover the hills and fall to the ground are called the snow of April, also known as May snow.
The Tung Blossom Festival, organized by the Hakka Affairs Council, began in 2002 to promote Hakka culture and tourism.
Festival events take place in many counties, including the Hakka areas of Hsinchu and Miaoli, and visitors hike mountain trails to see the flowers.
